questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Problem Secularism Answers' refers to.
questions.a: Where several religions share one country, the state must decide how to treat them all. If it privileges one faith, the others become second-class; if it persecutes all religion, believers lose their freedom. Secularism names the third path: a state that keeps equal distance from, and equal respect for, every religion.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Problem Secularism Answers'.
questions.a: One state, many faiths -- secularism is the discipline of equal respect, not the erasure of religion.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Problem Secularism Answers' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps108.txt lines 1-90 (introduction, coexistence of communities, the question of equal treatment by the state))

concepts.title: What is Secularism: Principled Distance and Equal Respect

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'What is Secularism: Principled Distance and Equal Respect' refers to.
questions.a: Secularism requires the state to have no religion of its own while treating all religions with equal respect. Its distinctive idea is principled distance: the state neither allies with any faith nor rigidly ignores religion, but intervenes or abstains in each case according to constitutional values of equality and freedom.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'What is Secularism: Principled Distance and Equal Respect'.
questions.a: Neither temple, church nor mosque holds state power -- yet the state may act on religion to protect equality and freedom.

questions.q: Under which section is 'What is Secularism: Principled Distance and Equal Respect' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps108.txt lines 90-170 (definition of secularism, separation of religion and state, principled distance, equal respect, intervention for reform))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Secularism and the Indian Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution embeds secularism without using one established creed: no state religion exists, Articles 25 to 28 guarantee freedom of conscience and religion subject to public order and rights, Articles 29 and 30 protect minority cultural and educational institutions, and the state may regulate secular aspects of religious practice.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Secularism and the Indian Constitution'.
questions.a: Freedom of religion plus minority protection plus no state faith -- the constitutional triangle of Indian secularism.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Secularism and the Indian Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps108.txt lines 170-260 (constitutional provisions, articles 25 to 28 freedom of religion, articles 29 and 30 cultural and educational rights, no state religion))

concepts.title: Criticisms of Secularism and the Communal Alternative

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Criticisms of Secularism and the Communal Alternative' refers to.
questions.a: Critics charge secularism with being anti-religious, a western import, or a mask for minoritism; defenders reply that principled distance neither attacks faith nor favours any community. The rival -- communalism -- assigns political loyalty by religion and has repeatedly produced discrimination and violence, the very disease secular institutions exist to prevent.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Criticisms of Secularism and the Communal Alternative'.
questions.a: Secularism is not godlessness; its real alternative is communal politics, which costs minorities and majorities alike.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Criticisms of Secularism and the Communal Alternative' taught, and from which source text?
